Paper notes · built from zero · no CUDA assumed

ThunderKittens ⚡

A complete, beginner-friendly walkthrough of “ThunderKittens: Simple, Fast, and Adorable AI Kernels” — what every word means, why it matters, and how to talk about it.

Paper: Spector, Arora, Singhal, Fu, Ré · Stanford · Oct 2024 arXiv: 2410.20399 You: starting at zero

These notes assume you have never written a GPU kernel and have never opened a CUDA file. We build the whole mental model from the ground up — what a GPU is, how it runs code, where the bottlenecks live — and only then read the paper. By the end you should be able to explain the paper to someone else, which is the real test of understanding.

How to read this: the core ideas live in Parts 1–4. Parts 0 and 5 are orientation and takeaways. The appendices are reference material — a deep-dive on memory layouts (the prettiest figures in the paper) and a full glossary you can scan whenever a term trips you up. Coloured boxes flag analogies, key insights, things to watch out for, and jargon.

Part 00

The 90-second version

Modern AI models are giant stacks of a few mathematical operations — matrix multiplies, attention, convolutions. Each operation has to be turned into an actual program that runs on a graphics card (a GPU). That program is called a kernel. Writing a kernel that runs near the hardware’s top speed is shockingly hard, even for the most important operations and the best engineers.

The paper makes a bet: instead of giving programmers a huge, complicated toolbox (NVIDIA’s CUTLASS) or a simple-but-limited one (compilers like Triton), maybe a small, opinionated set of just three abstractions — one for each level of the GPU — is enough to write kernels that are both easy to read and state-of-the-art fast. They build that library, call it ThunderKittens (TK), and show it works.

=
Matches NVIDIA CuBLAS on matrix multiply, in 40 lines
=
Matches FlashAttention-3 on attention
14×
Faster on linear attention
<1MB
Whole library, vs CuBLAS at 689 MB

The kicker: parts of TK were written by undergraduates who had never written CUDA, and the library is in production at AI-inference companies and high-frequency-trading firms. The thesis — “a few good abstractions go a long way” — held up.

The one sentence to remember

A GPU has a small amount of blisteringly fast specialized math hardware (tensor cores) and a lot of overhead around it; a great kernel is one that keeps that math hardware fed and busy while hiding everything else. ThunderKittens gives you three tools — one per level of the GPU — that make doing this simple.

Part 01

Why kernels are the bottleneck

What is a “kernel,” really?

When you run a neural network, the framework (PyTorch, say) breaks your model into operations: “multiply these two matrices,” “run attention over this sequence,” “apply this activation.” Each of those operations is dispatched to the GPU as a kernel — a small program that the thousands of cores on the GPU all run at once.

A kernel always follows the same rhythm: load data from the GPU’s main memory into fast on-chip memory, compute on it, then store the answer back to main memory. That’s it. The art is in doing this without wasting time.

Jargon, first pass
GPU
Graphics Processing Unit. Originally for rendering games; now the workhorse of AI because it can do thousands of arithmetic operations in parallel. The paper uses NVIDIA’s H100 as its reference chip.
Kernel
The actual GPU program for one operation. Not the “kernel” of an operating system, and not a “kernel function” in math — same word, different worlds.
FLOP / FLOP/s
A FLOP is one floating-point arithmetic operation (one multiply or add). FLOP/s is how many you do per second — the unit of raw speed. “TFLOP/s” = trillions per second. Every chart in this paper measures TFLOP/s; higher is better.
BF16
“Brain float 16” — a 16-bit number format. Using fewer bits per number lets the hardware crunch more numbers per second, which is why AI loves it.

The problem: a huge gap between possible and actual

Hardware has a theoretical top speed. Real kernels rarely get close. The paper’s motivating example is sobering: FlashAttention-2, a celebrated attention kernel, lost 47% of its performance when the H100 GPU came out — the code that was fast on the old chip was slow on the new one. It took the field over two years to produce FlashAttention-3 and recover that speed.

Meanwhile there’s been a “Cambrian explosion” of new model architectures (Mamba, linear attention, state-space models, and so on). Each one needs its own fast kernels, and writing them is a specialist craft. The mismatch between “new ideas” and “someone willing to spend two years hand-optimizing a kernel for them” is a real brake on AI progress. That brake is what the paper is trying to release.

The existing tools, and the gap TK aims at

There are two camps, and they trade off ease against power:

  • C++ libraries — CUTLASS / CuTe (NVIDIA). Extremely powerful and fast, but built from “a myriad of nested templates.” The learning curve is brutal; even experts find them hard, and — the paper shows — even kernels written with CUTLASS (like FlashAttention-3) still have avoidable inefficiencies.
  • Compilers — Triton, XLA, TVM, PyTorch. Much friendlier interfaces. But they’re not “embedded in C++,” so when you need an exotic hardware instruction or fine control over memory, you can hit a wall you can’t climb over.
The research question

How far can you get with a small set of opinionated abstractions — and does being concise force you to sacrifice speed? The whole paper is an answer to those two questions. (Spoiler: surprisingly far; and no.)

Part 02

GPU 101 — building the mental model

This is the part that makes everything else make sense. Take it slowly. A GPU is organized as a hierarchy, and so is its memory, and almost every performance idea in the paper is about respecting that hierarchy.

2.1 — Who does the work: the execution hierarchy

A GPU is a city of tiny workers organized into nested groups. From smallest to largest:

The execution hierarchy · who does the work
  • Thread (also “lane”). The smallest worker. It runs instructions and holds a little private scratch space called registers.
  • Warp = 32 threads. Here’s the crucial, non-obvious part: the 32 threads in a warp execute the same instruction at the same time, in lockstep, just on different pieces of data. A warp is the real atomic unit of execution. (Sometimes 4 warps are bundled into a warpgroup = 128 threads, which matters for the H100’s big matrix instructions.)
  • Block = a team of warps on one core. Warps are grouped into a thread block, which runs on one physical core called an SM (Streaming Multiprocessor). All the warps in a block can talk to each other quickly through fast shared memory. You can pack up to 64 warps onto one SM; how many you pack is called occupancy.
  • Grid = all the blocks on the whole GPU. The H100 has 132 SMs, so it can run 132 blocks truly simultaneously. Blocks on different SMs can only communicate through slow main memory.
Analogy — a restaurant at full tilt

A thread is one cook. A warp is a line of 32 cooks who all do the exact same motion on command (“everyone, dice your onion — now!”). A block/SM is one kitchen station with a shared prep counter the cooks can reach. The grid/GPU is the whole restaurant with 132 kitchen stations. Cooks at the same station share a counter (fast); cooks at different stations have to send runners to the central pantry (slow).

Two terms you’ll see constantly
SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)
One physical core of the GPU. The H100 has 132. A thread block runs on one SM.
Occupancy
How many warps you’ve packed onto an SM. More warps = more chances to overlap work and hide waiting — up to a point, because they compete for limited resources (this trade-off is a recurring theme).

2.2 — Where the data lives: the memory hierarchy

The single most important fact about GPU performance: memory comes in tiers, and they trade size against speed. Tiny memory is absurdly fast; huge memory is comparatively slow. Moving data between tiers is often what dominates a kernel’s runtime.

The memory hierarchy · size traded against speed
Analogy — where you keep your stuff

Registers are what’s in your hands right now — instant, but you can only hold a couple of things. Shared memory is your desktop — fast to reach, fits a working set. L2 cache is a shelf across the room — a few steps away. HBM (main memory) is a warehouse across town — it holds everything, but every trip costs you. Good kernels make as few warehouse trips as possible and do as much work as they can on the desk.

Here is the paper’s own version of that pyramid, on the left of its overview figure — note the exact numbers (size and bandwidth) for the H100, and the names ThunderKittens gives to data living at each level (rt = register tile, st = shared tile):

2.3 — The execution units, and why tensor cores rule everything

Inside each warp, instructions run on specialized execution units. Different units do different jobs and can run at the same time:

  • Load/Store units — move data between registers and memory. The H100 adds dedicated hardware (TMA) for moving big bulk chunks efficiently.
  • General compute — the ALU (comparisons like max/min), the FMA unit (multiply-and-add), and the XU (“special function unit” for expensive things like exp, used in softmax).
  • Tensor cores — dedicated matrix-multiply hardware. This is where almost all of a GPU’s compute power lives.

How much does it dominate? On the A100 and H100, the tensor cores deliver about 16× the FLOP/s of all the general-purpose math units combined.

Why tensor cores rule everything
The thesis, stated precisely

Because tensor cores are ~16× faster than everything else, a high-performance kernel must keep the tensor cores busy as much as possible, and minimize the overhead of all the non-tensor-core work (the memory loads, the exp in softmax, the bookkeeping). This single idea — feed the tensor cores, hide the rest — is the heart of the whole paper. Every ThunderKittens abstraction exists to serve it.

2.4 — The villains: where time gets wasted

Knowing the hierarchy, we can name the specific ways kernels go slow. The paper’s techniques are basically a list of fixes for these.

Villain #1 — Bank conflicts

Shared memory isn’t one big pool; it’s split into 32 “banks” that can be read in parallel — one lane per bank, all at once, if you’re lucky. But if several threads in a warp try to read from the same bank at the same time, the hardware can’t do them together: it serializes the accesses, one after another. That’s a bank conflict, and it quietly throttles your memory bandwidth.

Bank conflicts · the layout decides

Whether you get conflicts depends entirely on the layout — how your data’s logical positions map onto physical banks. Choosing layouts is fiddly and error-prone, and (the paper shows) even FlashAttention-3 leaves bank conflicts on the table. Making layouts automatic and correct is one of TK’s biggest selling points. We’ll see the gorgeous layout figures in Appendix A.

Villain #2 — Pipeline bubbles & launch overhead

Starting a thread block has a fixed setup-and-teardown cost. A kernel that keeps launching fresh blocks pays that tax over and over — idle gaps called pipeline bubbles.

Villain #3 — The tail effect

The GPU runs blocks in “waves” of 132 (one per SM). If your work doesn’t divide evenly, the last wave is mostly empty. The paper’s vivid example: a job of 133 blocks on 132 SMs takes two waves — the first runs at full efficiency, the second runs one block while 131 SMs sit idle (under 1% efficiency). Sizing the grid well matters.

Villain #4 — Synchronization stalls

Warps periodically have to wait at barriers for each other (“nobody move until everyone’s done loading”). While waiting, they do no useful work.

2.5 — The cost model: reduce, then overlap

The paper sums all this up in one tidy formula. Total time is the maximum of your memory costs and compute costs (because, ideally, they happen at the same time), plus the unavoidable overhead:

The cost model
Coverall = max( memory costs , compute costs ) + overhead
where memory = HBM + L2 + L1 + shared, and compute = tensor cores + ALU + FMA + XU. The max is the dream of perfect overlap; reality lands somewhere between the max and the sum.

This gives you exactly two levers to pull, and the paper organizes its whole toolkit around them:

  1. Reduce each individual cost (e.g., touch HBM less; avoid bank conflicts).
  2. Overlap the costs so they run concurrently instead of in sequence — turning a sum into a max.
Reduce, then overlap · turning a sum into a max
Part 03

The three ThunderKittens ideas

One abstraction per level of the GPU. That’s the whole library.

GPU levelThe problem thereTK’s abstraction
Warp
(32 threads)		Picking layouts that avoid bank conflicts and keep tensor cores happyTiles with auto-managed layouts + PyTorch-like operations
Block
(one SM)		Overlapping memory and compute across many warpsThe LCSF template (Load-Compute-Store-Finish)
Grid
(whole GPU)		Launch overhead, tail effects, reusing the L2 cachePersistent grids + block-launch ordering

3.1 — Warp level: tiles & PyTorch-like operations

TK’s two foundational ideas are tiles (the data) and bulk operations on tiles (the verbs), modeled deliberately on PyTorch/NumPy so they feel familiar.

The basic unit of data is a 16×16 tile of numbers. Why 16×16? Because that’s the shape the tensor cores want to chew on — building everything out of these tiles maximizes the chance you’re using the fast hardware. TK gives you a tile type for each memory tier:

  • rt<M,N> — a register tile (lives in the fastest memory), templated by its number type, shape, and layout.
  • st<M,N> — a shared tile (lives in shared memory).
  • gl<...> — a global layout descriptor, describing a big 4-D tensor in main memory (think {batch, head, length, embedding}, like a PyTorch tensor) that you’ll load tiles out of.

On top of tiles you get a tidy set of parallel operations with PyTorch-y names: mma (matrix-multiply-accumulate), exp, mul, add, sub_row, row_max, cumsum, and so on. A whole warp (or warpgroup) cooperatively executes one of these on a tile.

Why this is more than “nice syntax”

Because tiles carry their shape and layout in the type system, TK can check correctness at compile time. GPU kernels are notoriously hard to debug; here, if you try to feed a tensor-core multiply two tiles in the wrong layouts, you get a compile error instead of a silently-wrong-or-slow result. And TK auto-selects the best memory layout for each tile (the swizzling from Appendix A) so you never hand-tune banks. The abstraction is doing real safety and performance work for you.

See it side by side: attention in PyTorch vs. ThunderKittens

This is Figure 2 of the paper, and it’s the best single illustration of the “feels like PyTorch” claim. On the left, attention in PyTorch. On the right, the same math in TK. Read them in parallel — the operations line up almost one-to-one.

PyTorch

 attention (PyTorch)
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F

# compute Q @ K.T
att = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(2,3))

# softmax over the scores
att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1,
                dtype=torch.float32)

# back to bf16
att = att.to(q.dtype)

# multiply by V
out = torch.matmul(att, v)

ThunderKittens

 attention (TK)
using namespace kittens;
rt_bf<16,64> k_reg, v_reg;

// Q @ K.T  (on tensor cores)
zero(att);
mma_ABt(att, q_reg, k_reg, att);

// softmax = sub max, exp, divide
sub_row(att, att, max_vec);
exp(att, att);
div_row(att, att, norm_vec);

// att @ V  (on tensor cores)
copy(att_mma, att);
mma_AB(o_reg, att_mma, v_reg, o_reg);

The TK code is doing the same three things — score = Q·Kᵀ, softmax, output = scores·V — using tile operations. The extra lines (zero, copy, load) are the cost of being explicit about where data lives, which is exactly the control that lets it run fast. The two mma calls are the ones that hit the tensor cores; everything else is the “overhead” we’re trying to keep cheap.

3.2 — Block level: the LCSF template

At the block level the goal is overlap: while some warps wait on a slow memory load, other warps should be computing. TK provides a single reusable scaffold for this, called the LCSF template — for its four steps, Load, Compute, Store, Finish. It’s built on a classic idea called the producer–consumer pattern.

Analogy — a kitchen line

Split your warps into two crews. Producers (“load/store workers”) do nothing but ferry ingredients from the warehouse (HBM) to the prep counter (shared memory) and carry finished plates back. Consumers (“compute workers”) never leave the counter — they just cook (run tensor cores and math) on whatever ingredients are ready. Because the runners fetch the next batch while the cooks work on the current one, nobody stands idle. That overlap is the whole point.

The LCSF template · producers, buffers, consumers

To use the template, you fill in four small functions and TK handles the hard parts:

  1. Load — which data to bring from HBM into shared memory, and when to signal “ready.”
  2. Compute — the actual math, written with the tile operations from §3.1.
  3. Store — which results to write back to HBM.
  4. Finish — clean up and write any final state.

Here’s what the load and compute functions look like for attention (this is Figure 5 of the paper). The producer issues asynchronous loads; the consumer does the matmul-softmax-matmul and signals when it’s done with the inputs:

Load function (producer)

 load
if (warpgroup::warpid() == 0) {
  tma::expect(inputs_arrived,
              block.k, block.v);
  tma::load_async(
     block.k, globals.k,
     {batch, head, iter, 0},
     inputs_arrived);
  tma::load_async(
     block.v, globals.v,
     {batch, head, iter, 0},
     inputs_arrived);
}
else arrive(inputs_arrived);

Compute function (consumer)

 compute
warpgroup::mm_ABt(att,
   scratch.q[state.id], block.k);
warpgroup::mma_async_wait();

// softmax (simplified)
sub_row(att, att, max_vec);
exp(att, att);
div_row(att, att, norm_vec);

copy(att_bf16, att);

warpgroup::mma_AB(state.o,
   att_bf16, block.v);
warpgroup::mma_async_wait();
arrive(inputs_finished);

Three pieces of machinery do the heavy lifting so you don’t have to:

Multi-stage buffers (the pipeline)

The template keeps an N-stage buffer in shared memory. With 1 stage, loaders must wait for cooks to finish before refilling — no overlap. With 2 stages, the next tile loads while the current one cooks. Deeper buffers overlap even more. You set one number — the number of stages — and TK manages the rest. The payoff is large:

Synchronization barriers

Producers must tell consumers “new data is ready”; consumers must tell producers “I’m done, you can refill.” TK exposes a single arrive() call for a worker to announce it finished its step, and wires up the barriers behind the scenes.

Asynchronous I/O

TK wraps both the older async-copy instruction (cp.async) and the H100’s bulk-transfer hardware (TMA) behind one interface, and auto-generates the descriptors TMA needs. You write load_async; TK picks the fast path.

Jargon — the H100 acceleration instructions
TMA (Tensor Memory Accelerator)
Dedicated H100 hardware for moving big blocks between HBM and shared memory without tying up the regular compute threads. TK uses it automatically.
WGMMA
A “warpgroup matrix-multiply-accumulate” — the H100’s big asynchronous tensor-core instruction that a whole warpgroup (128 threads) issues together, streaming straight from shared memory. The baselines in the paper that don’t use TMA/WGMMA are exactly the ones TK beats most.
Producer–consumer
A classic concurrency pattern: some workers produce items into a shared buffer, others consume them, decoupled by the buffer so neither waits on the other. Dates back to Dijkstra, 1968.

The occupancy trade-off — and why a template helps

Remember occupancy (how many warps per SM)? More workers means more overlap — but they fight over registers and shared memory, so past a point, performance falls. Because TK lets you change the worker count trivially, you can find the sweet spot. The paper compares a naïve synchronous kernel against an LCSF one across occupancies:

What the occupancy chart is telling you

Both kernels rise then fall — that’s the contention effect. But the async LCSF kernel reaches a much higher peak (it “expands the Pareto frontier,” in the paper’s words). It also peaks at a lower occupancy, because good overlap means you don’t need to brute-force it with more warps. The template turns a hard hand-tuning problem into “try a few numbers.”

3.3 — Grid level: launching blocks wisely

At the top level, TK doesn’t force a grid structure on you, but it shows two big, free wins.

Persistent grids — stop paying the launch tax

Instead of launching a new block for every chunk of work (and paying setup/teardown each time → pipeline bubbles), launch exactly 132 blocks once — one per SM — and have each block loop, pulling the next chunk of work itself. You can even prefetch the next chunk’s data into the buffer while finishing the current one. The paper’s GEMM gets a steady few-percent bump from this:

Persistent grids · stop paying the launch tax
K dimensionTK — relaunchTK — persistentCuBLAS

256271309242
512414450407
1024565600633
 Table 2. Persistent launch (TFLOP/s) for TK GEMM, M=N=4096, as K varies. Persistent (teal) beats relaunch at every size, and beats CuBLAS until the largest K.

Block launch order — squeezing the L2 cache

Blocks talk through HBM (slow) — but if two blocks need the same data and run close together in time, the second finds that data still sitting in the L2 cache (fast). Whether that happens depends on the order you launch blocks in, because the cache evicts old data. Reordering blocks so neighbours-in-time share data can dramatically cut HBM traffic. The effect is huge:

KernelBlock orderHBM read (GB/s)Speed (TFLOP/s)
GEMM 16384³{8, N, M/8} — tiled982805
GEMM 16384³{N, M} — row-major3,070392
Attention D=128{N, H, B}213600
Attention D=128{B, H, N}2,390494
 Table 3. Same kernel, same math — only the launch order changes. The bad order reads 3× more from HBM and runs at half the speed. Lower HBM traffic = more cache reuse = faster.
A number worth internalizing

For a 16384³ matrix multiply, switching from a naïve row-major launch order to a tiled one took the kernel from 387 to 797 TFLOP/s — a >50% swing — with no change to the actual computation. At smaller sizes (that fit in L2) the effect nearly vanishes. Cache behaviour is invisible in the math but decisive in the speed; this is the kind of thing TK makes easy to explore.

Part 04

Does it actually work?

The claim is bold — “few abstractions, no speed lost.” So the experiments matter. All benchmarks are on an NVIDIA H100 80GB, measured in TFLOP/s (higher is better). The charts below are re-drawn from the paper’s numbers.

The workhorses: GEMM and attention

These two operations power the Transformer and have absorbed years of industry optimization. Beating them isn’t the goal — matching them with far simpler code is.

Read the attention story carefully

On the forward pass, TK ties FA3 — and it does so without FA3’s clever hand-built “ping-pong scheduler.” On the backward pass (which is harder and less optimized everywhere), TK wins by 10–40%. The lesson isn’t “TK is magic”; it’s “a clean template recovers expert-level performance, and on the less-trodden paths it pulls ahead.”

The new architectures: where simple abstractions pay off most

This is the real prize. New model types (state-space models, linear attention, FFT convolutions) usually have weak kernels because nobody’s hand-optimized them yet. TK makes writing a good kernel for them fast — so the speedups are dramatic.

The pattern across all of these

Look at how the TK bars stay flat or rise as sequences get longer, while baselines often sag. That’s TK keeping the tensor cores fed at scale and overlapping memory, instead of getting starved. The baselines (mostly Triton or plain PyTorch) leave the tensor cores idle for these less-common operations; TK doesn’t. Up to 14× on Based linear attention, ~6.5× on Hedgehog, >3× on Mamba-2, 4.7–8.7× on long convolution.

Looking under the hood: the profiler doesn’t lie

Speed charts show that TK is faster; profiling shows why. Using NVIDIA’s NSight Compute tool, the paper compares hardware-utilization metrics directly:

FlashFFTConv13.425.514.81.6
ThunderKittens (conv)54.840.031.40.3
 Table 4. Profiles from NSight Compute. Two findings stand out (next).
  • No bank conflicts. On attention-backward, TK and FA3 use the tensor cores about equally — but TK has 85% fewer shared-memory stalls. The profiler reports up to 9.6-way bank conflicts in FA3; TK has effectively none. That’s the automatic-layout abstraction (§3.1) earning its keep.
  • Tensor cores actually used. On long convolution, FlashFFTConv leaves the tensor cores at 13% utilization; TK runs them at 55% — a 4.1× jump — by expressing the FFT math as matrix multiplies that hit the tensor cores (via WGMMA). The baseline simply wasn’t using the fast hardware.

Simplicity isn’t only about lines of code — it’s about the whole footprint a developer has to reason about.

Part 05

Why it matters & what to take away

Strip away the details and the paper is making one disciplined argument, and backing it with evidence:

The argument in full

The GPU looks like it demands a sprawling toolbox of techniques. But map the right small abstraction onto each level of the hardware hierarchy — tiles for the warp, an async template for the block, launch scheduling for the grid — and you can write kernels that are simultaneously simple to read and at or above the state of the art. Conciseness did not cost performance.

The consequences worth carrying with you:

  • Accessibility is the real product. Undergrads with no CUDA experience wrote competitive kernels. Lowering the barrier to high-performance AI code is arguably more important than any single benchmark, because it unblocks the long tail of new architectures.
  • It earns its place in production. TK is used by ML-inference providers and high-frequency-trading firms — the two communities that care most about squeezing GPUs. That’s a strong external validation.
  • “Embedded in C++” means it fails gracefully. Unlike a compiler (where an unsupported operation is a dead end), TK is a C++ library: when its abstractions don’t cover your case, you can drop down to raw CUDA in the same file. You get the simple path and the escape hatch.
  • The bottleneck framing is the takeaway. If you remember one thing for an interview: AI performance is gated by mapping architectures onto hardware, the lever is feeding the tensor cores while hiding memory latency, and the hard parts are layouts, overlap, and scheduling — one per level of the hierarchy.
Appendix A

Deep dive: shared-memory layouts

This is the visual heart of the paper, and the clearest example of a problem TK hides from you. Recall the goal: store a tile in shared memory so that (a) the 32 threads of a warp hit 32 different banks at once (no bank conflicts), and (b) the layout is still compatible with the H100’s fast hardware instructions (WGMMA, TMA). Those two goals fight each other, and the appendix walks through six attempts.

In every image below, each little cell is one element of a tile, the number is the memory bank it lands in (00–31), and the colour tracks the bank. The thing to look for: within any column that a warp reads together, are the banks all different (good) or repeated (conflict)?

The headline figure

Figure 4 from the paper packs four layouts into one image. Top-left is the naïve one (notice columns of the same colour → conflicts when feeding tensor cores). Top-right is the padded fix. The bottom two are layouts TK actually uses:

The six layouts, and their trade-offs

LayoutBank conflictsFast-instruction (WGMMA/TMA) support?Verdict
Naïve (row-major)8-wayyessimple, but conflicts make it very slow
Paddednoneno (misaligned addresses)fixes conflicts, breaks fast instructions
Naïve swizzle (XOR with row)nonenoclever, but still no hardware support
32-byte swizzle4-wayyesworks for any width × multiple of 16
64-byte swizzle2-wayyesneeds width multiple of 32
128-byte swizzlenoneyesbest — needs width multiple of 64
 The first three each fail one requirement. The last three (TK’s chosen family) keep hardware support while cutting conflicts — so TK ships exactly these and, at compile time, picks the strongest one a given tile’s width allows.
Jargon — “swizzling”

Swizzling means scrambling the mapping from logical position to physical address — here, by XOR-ing the address with some of its own bits — so that elements which would have collided in the same bank get spread across different banks instead. “32/64/128-byte” refers to how aggressive the scramble is. More aggressive = fewer conflicts but stricter requirements on tile width.

Seeing the progression

Watch the colour pattern change from “striped” (conflicts) to a “diagonal staircase” (banks spread out) as the swizzle gets more aggressive:

The payoff of all this: you never see any of it. You declare a tile, TK measures its width at compile time and silently picks 128/64/32-byte swizzling. The 85%-fewer-stalls result in Table 4 is this appendix, automated.

The massively parallel chip AI runs on. Reference here: NVIDIA H100 SXM (132 cores).
Kernel
A GPU program for one operation: load → compute → store.
Thread / lane
The smallest worker; has private registers.
Warp
32 threads that run the same instruction in lockstep. The true unit of execution.
Warpgroup
4 warps (128 threads) — the unit the H100’s big matrix instruction (WGMMA) operates on.
Block / thread block
A group of warps that runs on one SM and shares fast memory.
SM (Streaming Multiprocessor)
One physical core. The H100 has 132.
Grid
All the blocks launched for a kernel, spread across the GPU.
Occupancy
How many warps are packed onto an SM. More = more overlap, but more resource contention.
Tensor core
Specialized matrix-multiply hardware holding ~16× the FLOP/s of general compute. Keeping it busy is the whole game.
ALU / FMA / XU
General compute units: comparisons (ALU), multiply-add (FMA), special functions like exp (XU).
Tail effect
Wasted capacity when work doesn’t divide evenly into waves of 132 blocks.
Pipeline bubble
Idle time from block setup/teardown overhead.
Memory
HBM (High-Bandwidth Memory)
Main GPU memory. Biggest (80 GB) and slowest (3 TB/s). Touch it as little as possible.
L2 cache
A shared on-chip cache (50 MB, 12 TB/s). Reusing data here instead of HBM is a big win.
Shared memory (SMEM) / L1
Per-block fast memory (227 KB, 33 TB/s), split into 32 banks.
Registers
Per-thread, fastest memory (64 KB, 130 TB/s). The H100 caps it at 255 per thread; overflow “spills” to slower memory.
Bank / bank conflict
Shared memory’s 32 parallel lanes. A conflict is when threads hit the same bank at once and get serialized → slow.
Swizzling
Scrambling addresses (via XOR) to spread data across banks and avoid conflicts.
Layout
How logical data elements map to physical thread/bank ownership. Wrong layout = conflicts or no tensor-core support.
Software, instructions & operations
ThunderKittens (TK)
The library this paper introduces.
CUDA
NVIDIA’s low-level GPU programming language/platform (a C++ dialect).
CUTLASS / CuTe
NVIDIA’s powerful-but-complex C++ template libraries for GPU linear algebra.
Triton
A popular compiler-based framework with a simpler (Python-like) interface, fewer low-level controls.
CuBLAS
NVIDIA’s hand-tuned matrix-multiply (GEMM) library — the GEMM gold standard (689 MB).
Tile
TK’s core data structure: a 16×16 block of numbers. rt = register tile, st = shared tile, gl = global descriptor.
LCSF template
TK’s block-level scaffold: Load, Compute, Store, Finish — fill four functions, get overlap for free.
Producer–consumer
Splitting workers into data-movers and computers, decoupled by a buffer.
Pipeline / multi-stage buffer
Multiple shared-memory slots so the next tile loads while the current one computes.
TMA
Tensor Memory Accelerator: H100 hardware for fast bulk HBM↔SMEM transfers.
cp.async
The older asynchronous-copy instruction; TK wraps it and TMA behind one interface.
WGMMA
Warpgroup matrix-multiply-accumulate — the H100’s async tensor-core instruction.
GEMM
GEneral Matrix-Matrix multiply — the most fundamental dense operation in AI.
mma / mma_AB / mma_ABt
TK’s matrix-multiply-accumulate ops (the t means one input is transposed).
Attention
The Transformer’s core operation: score = Q·Kᵀ, softmax, output = scores·V. “Causal” = each token only sees earlier ones; “backward” = the gradient pass used in training.
Linear attention / SSM / FFT convolution
Newer, often cheaper alternatives to standard attention — the architectures where TK’s speedups are largest because nobody had hand-tuned their kernels yet.
FlashAttention-2 / -3
State-of-the-art attention kernels; FA3 is TK’s main attention baseline.
Appendix C

How to go deeper

Since you mentioned using this as job-prep reading, here’s a sensible path from “I understand this paper” to “I can work in this area.” You don’t need all of it — pick based on how hands-on you want to get.

If you want to be able to discuss it (interviews, reading more papers)

  • Be fluent in the hierarchy story: thread→warp→block→grid, and registers→shared→L2→HBM. Most kernel discussions are some variation of “which level is the bottleneck and why.”
  • Be able to state the tensor-core thesis and the cost model in your own words (Parts 2.3–2.5 above).
  • Know the three named villains people optimize against: bank conflicts, lack of overlap, and bad scheduling/L2 reuse.
  • Read the FlashAttention papers next — they’re the canonical “IO-aware kernel” story and the baseline TK compares to. The original (Dao et al., 2022) is the most readable.

If you want to get hands-on

  • The ThunderKittens code is open source at github.com/HazyResearch/ThunderKittens. Reading the GEMM and attention kernels in the appendix alongside the repo is the single best way to make this concrete.
  • Learn just enough CUDA to understand a “hello world” kernel and the idea of threads/blocks — you don’t need to master raw CUDA, just enough to see what TK is abstracting away.
  • Get comfortable with profiling as a habit (NVIDIA NSight Compute, as in Table 4). “Look at the profile before optimizing” is the whole culture in one sentence.
The mental test of understanding

Could you explain to a friend, without notes: why is a GPU fast, why are kernels hard to write, and what are the three things ThunderKittens does about it? If yes, you’ve got the paper. If a part is fuzzy, that’s the section to re-read.

Source paper: B. F. Spector, S. Arora, A. Singhal, D. Y. Fu, C. Ré. “ThunderKittens: Simple, Fast, and Adorable AI Kernels.” Stanford University, 27 Oct 2024. arXiv:2410.20399. Code: HazyResearch/ThunderKittens.
